title: Connecting Applications to Databases
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of connecting applications to databases.
Choose and interpret a suitable Docker example connected to connecting applications to databases.
Predict an expected result and verify it using observable evidence in a controlled environment.

content.intro: This lesson covers Connecting Applications to Databases. You will connect the named subtopics from the supplied Docker curriculum to a small, observable example. Work through the visual first, then use the example to form a prediction and check it against the actual behavior.
content.why_it_matters: A real application is a set of processes with dependencies and lifecycles. Each service should have a clear role, a reproducible image, configuration from the environment, network access limited to its dependencies, health/diagnostic behavior, and explicit persistence where state must survive. Learning connecting applications to databases helps you make deployment behavior explicit and repeatable instead of relying on a command that happened to work on one machine.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: A real application is a set of processes with dependencies and lifecycles. Each service should have a clear role, a reproducible image, configuration from the environment, network access limited to its dependencies, health/diagnostic behavior, and explicit persistence where state must survive.

items.title: Database service discovery
items.text: Service discovery lets a container resolve a peer by a network-scoped name or alias. Names resolve only where the relevant network and service configuration make them visible.

items.title: Hostnames and ports
items.text: A container port and a published host port are different values. Bind publishing deliberately, especially when a service should be reachable only from the local machine.

items.title: Connection credentials
items.text: A secret needs a restricted path from its source to the process that needs it. Avoid putting it in images, normal build arguments, source control, or diagnostic output.

items.title: Startup and health checks
items.text: A health check tests a defined condition; it must reflect meaningful application readiness and can be wrong if its command or target is inappropriate.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming that a successful start means the application is ready.
common_mistakes.why: A container can start while its dependent service is unavailable or the application is failing after startup.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect health/status and logs; add a meaningful health check or retry strategy where appropriate.

common_mistakes.problem: Keeping required data only in the container writable layer.
common_mistakes.why: Replacing the container can discard that layer and its application state.
common_mistakes.fix: Select a named volume or an external storage system, then rehearse a restore.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a command without checking context, target, or permissions.
common_mistakes.why: Docker commands affect the active endpoint and can change host resources or publish services.
common_mistakes.fix: Check `docker context show`, use an isolated lab, make the smallest change, and verify the resulting state.
